canonical_statement: The primary aim was to characterize the epidemiology and identify risk factors for overall, viral, bacterial, and severe (grade >=3) infections associated with bispecific antibody therapy for multiple myeloma.

Secondary aims were to assess infections during the first cytokine release syndrome episode and the impact of baseline immunosuppression, comorbidities, and intravenous immunoglobulin therapy on infection risk.
The cohort included all adults with multiple myeloma who received bispecific antibody therapy at University Hospital 12 de Octubre from January 2020 through May 2025.

population.label: Adults with multiple myeloma treated with bispecific antibodies at the study center
inclusion_criteria: Received bispecific antibody therapy from January 2020 to May 2025

canonical_statement: Patients were identified from a prospective hematologic malignancy registry, with variables not already registered collected retrospectively from electronic health records into a standardized database.
Infectious events were recorded from bispecific antibody initiation until one month after discontinuation or initiation of a new therapy line, whichever occurred first.
Severe hypogammaglobulinemia was defined as IgG below 400 mg/dL after subtracting the monoclonal component attributable to multiple myeloma.

outcome.definition: IgG <400 mg/dL after subtraction of the monoclonal component

canonical_statement: A proven bacterial infection required isolation of a potentially pathogenic microorganism from a clinical specimen together with compatible local or systemic signs of infection.

outcome.definition: Potential pathogen isolated from a clinical specimen plus compatible local or systemic infection signs

canonical_statement: A probable bacterial infection required compatible signs and symptoms without an isolated pathogen and complete resolution after empiric antibiotic therapy.

outcome.definition: Compatible signs and symptoms, no isolated pathogen, and complete resolution after empiric antibiotic therapy

canonical_statement: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) were excluded from the infection analysis.
All patients were prescribed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg three times weekly or monthly intravenous pentamidine.

exposures.details: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg three times weekly or monthly intravenous pentamidine

canonical_statement: All patients were prescribed herpesvirus prophylaxis with acyclovir 800 mg twice daily.
Patients with severe hypogammaglobulinemia received intravenous immunoglobulin replacement at 0.4 g/kg monthly.
Incidence rates were calculated as infection episodes per bispecific antibody course-year with 95% confidence intervals.

Risk factors for infection were analyzed with recurrent-event Cox regression; intravenous immunoglobulin was treated as a time-dependent covariate, and variables with univariate P<0.10 were eligible for multivariable modeling.
A Fine-Gray competing-risk sensitivity analysis treated death as the competing event and reported subdistribution hazard ratios.
The 98 bispecific antibody courses had a mean patient age of 63.3 years (SD 10.7).

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that bispecific antibody therapy in multiple myeloma carries a high infection burden dominated by respiratory and gastrointestinal infections.

The authors interpreted cumulative immunosuppression from prior therapies, comorbidities, and ICANS as major determinants of infection risk, with intravenous immunoglobulin therapy appearing protective.
The authors concluded that antibiotic stewardship is feasible during early CRS episodes, when bacterial infection was uncommon, while later severe CRS/ICANS warrants greater infection vigilance.

The authors suggested that routine antifungal prophylaxis beyond Pneumocystis prophylaxis may not be necessary in this population, based on the low frequency of opportunistic fungal infections observed.
Meaningful comparisons between individual bispecific antibody agents were not feasible because of the observational design and heterogeneity of patient profiles.
Data on individual bispecific antibody dose modifications due to concurrent infections were unavailable.
The single-center design limits external validity because local epidemiology may shape the observed infection spectrum.
Incomplete electronic health record data prevented accurate determination of the duration of lymphopenia and neutropenia during individual treatment courses.
Vaccination status was not collected, preventing evaluation of the potential protective effect of vaccination practices.
The high frequency of upper respiratory viral infections may have diluted the relative proportion of clinically significant severe infections.
Excluding cystitis may have omitted potentially relevant lower urinary tract infections.
Follow-up was censored at bispecific antibody discontinuation or initiation of a subsequent therapy line, so late-onset infections related to prior exposure may have been missed.
The COVID-19 pandemic context may limit generalizability to other time periods.
